PROFESSIONAL LLC PROHIBITION IN CALIFORNIA — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Consulting

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan T. Reyes, states what California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.01 et seq.) provides about a limited liability company's ability to render licensed "professional services" in California — a question that comes up for a licensed professional (for example, in law, medicine, accountancy, architecture, or another licensed field) who is considering the limited liability company as a business form. Where a specific profession or a specific proposed business name is named below, those are Law and Acme Consulting; this sheet can also be read on its own, without either filled in, as a general reference to what the statute says. This sheet is a companion to this project's separate Professional Corporation — Formation Information Sheet, which addresses the professional corporation form that many licensed professions use instead. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular profession, business plan, or proposed entity is or is not permitted to use the limited liability company form, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

GENERAL LAWFUL PURPOSE, AND A CONDITIONAL LICENSED-SERVICES CARVE-OUT
California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act states, as a general matter, that a limited liability company "may have any lawful purpose, regardless of whether for profit," subject to three named exclusions: the banking business, the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks, and the trust company business. The same subdivision then addresses licensed services directly: a domestic or foreign limited liability company "may render services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certificate, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act" — but only "if the applicable provisions" of that same body of law "authorize a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to hold that license, certificate, or registration." Read on its own, this is a conditional permission, not an automatic one: whether an LLC may render a given licensed service depends on what the specific licensing statute for that service itself says about an LLC holding the license — this subdivision does not, by itself, supply that authorization.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A limited liability company may have any lawful purpose, regardless of whether for profit, except the banking business, the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks, or the trust company business. A domestic or foreign limited liability company may render services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certificate, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act, if the applicable provisions of the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act authorize a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to hold that license, certificate, or registration."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.04(b), Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, general lawful-purpose provision and conditional licensed-services carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.04.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the general conditional structure Section 17701.04(b) itself sets out; it does not survey which, if any, specific licenses, certificates, or registrations under the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act currently authorize a limited liability company to hold them — that determination depends on each profession's own governing statute, which was not individually checked here. The next clause in this document addresses a separate, more narrowly defined category of services, to which subdivision (e) of this same section applies a different, unconditional rule. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and limited-liability-company requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.

UNCONDITIONAL BAR ON RENDERING "PROFESSIONAL SERVICES" AS DEFINED FOR THIS PURPOSE
A separate subdivision of the same section states a different and unconditional rule for a specifically cross-referenced category of services: "[n]othing in this title shall be construed to permit a domestic or foreign limited liability company to render professional services, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 13401 and in Section 13401.3, in this state." Unlike subdivision (b)'s conditional carve-out — which turns on what a particular profession's own governing statute separately says about an LLC holding a license — subdivision (e) does not leave that possibility open for the specific category of services it defines by cross-reference as "professional services." It states directly that nothing in the Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act ("this title") should be read as itself supplying, or as inviting an inference of, authorization for an LLC to render professional services in that defined sense. Which occupations actually fall within that defined category is addressed in the next clause of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Nothing in this title shall be construed to permit a domestic or foreign limited liability company to render professional services, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 13401 and in Section 13401.3, in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.04(e), Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, bar on rendering "professional services" as cross-referenced (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.04.)
  Known gap: Subdivisions (b) and (e) of Section 17701.04 are treated in this document as one primary source (both are part of the same statutory section, fetched and confirmed together), not as two independent sources — the description above of how they relate is this document's own reading of that one section's text, not a claim drawn from a second, independent authority. Section 17701.04 does not itself state, in so many words, that subdivision (e) "overrides" or otherwise interacts with subdivision (b) in any particular way for professional services as defined by Section 13401(a) and Section 13401.3; that description is a plain-text reading of the two subdivisions, not a conclusion drawn from any judicial or administrative interpretation, and no case law construing this specific relationship was located or reviewed as part of this verification pass. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and limited-liability-company requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.

"PROFESSIONAL SERVICES" DEFINED FOR THIS PURPOSE, BY CROSS-REFERENCE
The "professional services" that subdivision (e) places off-limits to a limited liability company are defined by cross-reference to two other statutes, not restated within Section 17701.04 itself. Cal. Corp. Code § 13401(a) — part of the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act — defines "[p]rofessional services" to mean "any type of professional services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, or the Osteopathic Act." Cal. Corp. Code § 13401.3 then adds one further category to that same definition, "[a]s used in this part": professional services "that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act." Together, these two sections supply the entire defined universe Section 17701.04(e) points to: a domestic or foreign LLC may not render any service that may lawfully be rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration under the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act. Because the Business and Professions Code separately licenses a very wide range of occupations, this defined category is broad by cross-reference, not limited to a short, fixed list of named professions written into Section 17701.04, Section 13401, or Section 13401.3 themselves.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "“Professional services” means any type of professional services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, or the Osteopathic Act."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13401(a), Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, definition of "professional services" cross-referenced by the LLC prohibition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13401.)
  "As used in this part, “professional services” also means any type of professional services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act (Article 2 (commencing with Section 700) of Chapter 5 of Division 3 of the Harbors and Navigation Code)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13401.3, Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, Yacht and Ship Brokers Act addition to the "professional services" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13401.3.)
  Known gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 13401(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 13401.3, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This clause identifies the statutory source of the "professional services" definition that Section 17701.04(e) cross-references; it does not itself catalog every specific license, certification, or registration under the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act that falls within that definition — that would require checking each individual licensing statute, which was not done here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and limited-liability-company requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.

ONE NARROW, NAMED EXCEPTION: A HEALTH CARE SERVICE PLAN SUBSIDIARY
Section 17701.04 itself supplies one specifically named exception to its general framework, though by its own terms it is framed as an exception to subdivision (b)'s lawful-purpose provision rather than as an exception to subdivision (e)'s professional-services bar. Subdivision (d) states that, "[n]otwithstanding subdivision (b) and as specifically provided in this subdivision, a limited liability company may operate as a health care service plan licensed pursuant to Chapter 2.2 (commencing with Section 1340) of Division 2 of the Health and Safety Code if the limited liability company is a subsidiary of a health care service plan licensed pursuant to those provisions and the limited liability company is established to serve an existing line of business of the parent health care service plan." The same subdivision adds a liability-specific rule for this narrow case: the tort or contract liability of such an LLC and its members "is not limited or restricted in any manner because of the limited liability company status of the health care service plan." This exception is narrow and specifically conditioned — it applies only to a health care service plan LLC that is a subsidiary of an already-licensed parent health care service plan and that serves an existing line of that parent's business — not to health care service plans generally, and not to an individual licensed professional organizing their own practice as an LLC.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (b) and as specifically provided in this subdivision, a limited liability company may operate as a health care service plan licensed pursuant to Chapter 2.2 (commencing with Section 1340) of Division 2 of the Health and Safety Code if the limited liability company is a subsidiary of a health care service plan licensed pursuant to those provisions and the limited liability company is established to serve an existing line of business of the parent health care service plan."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.04(d), Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, narrow health care service plan subsidiary exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17701.04.)

Code § 17701.04, and is treated as part of that same primary source, not as an independent citation. Subdivision (d) is framed by its own text as an exception to subdivision (b) ("[n]otwithstanding subdivision (b)"), not expressly to subdivision (e)'s professional-services bar; whether or how a health care service plan might separately fall within the "professional services" defined by Section 13401(a) and Section 13401.3 was not independently researched here, and this clause does not draw that conclusion either way. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and limited-liability-company requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.

CONTRAST: THE REGISTERED LIMITED LIABILITY PARTNERSHIP FORM IS AVAILABLE, BUT ONLY TO A NARROWER, NAMED SET OF PROFESSIONS
California law makes a different kind of limited-liability entity available to a specific, named set of licensed professions: the registered limited liability partnership. Cal. Corp. Code § 16951 states that "[f]or purposes of this chapter, the only types of limited liability partnerships that shall be recognized are a registered limited liability partnership and a foreign limited liability partnership, as defined in Section 16101," and adds directly that "[n]o registered limited liability partnership or foreign limited liability partnership may render professional limited liability partnership services in this state except through licensed persons." Cal. Corp. Code § 16101 in turn defines a "[r]egistered limited liability partnership," in relevant part, as a partnership formed under Article 10 and registered under Section 16953 that is either composed of partners individually licensed to provide professional limited liability partnership services, related to a qualifying partnership under specific conditions, or — the branch most relevant here — one that "is licensed under the laws of the state to engage in the practice of architecture, the practice of public accountancy, the practice of engineering, the practice of land surveying, or the practice of law." Unlike the limited liability company, which subdivision (e) of Section 17701.04 bars from rendering the broadly cross-referenced set of "professional services" defined by Section 13401(a) and Section 13401.3, the registered limited liability partnership form is affirmatively available under Section 16101 — but only to this specific, shorter, named list of professions, and even then only through the partnership's own licensed persons.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "For purposes of this chapter, the only types of limited liability partnerships that shall be recognized are a registered limited liability partnership and a foreign limited liability partnership, as defined in Section 16101. No registered limited liability partnership or foreign limited liability partnership may render professional limited liability partnership services in this state except through licensed persons."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16951, Registered limited liability partnerships, exclusive recognized types and licensed-persons requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16951.)
  "“Registered limited liability partnership” means a partnership, other than a limited partnership, formed pursuant to an agreement governed by Article 10 (commencing with Section 16951), that is registered under Section 16953 and (i) each of the partners of which is a licensed person or a person licensed or authorized to provide professional limited liability partnership services in a jurisdiction or jurisdictions other than this state, (ii) is licensed under the laws of the state to engage in the practice of architecture, the practice of public accountancy, the practice of engineering, the practice of land surveying, or the practice of law, or (iii)(I) is related to a registered limited liability partnership that practices public accountancy or, to the extent permitted by the State Bar of California, practices law or is related to a foreign limited liability partnership and (II) provides services related or complementary to the professional limited liability partnership services provided by, or provides services or facilities to, that registered limited liability partnership or foreign limited liability partnership."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16101(a)(8)(A), Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, definition of "registered limited liability partnership" and its named-profession licensing branch (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16101.)
  Known gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 16951 and Cal. Corp. Code § 16101, and are treated as two independent sources. As of this verification, the California Legislative Information website listed two different 2024-amended versions of Section 16101 on file (one reflecting Stats. 2024, Ch. 361, Sec. 9, and a separate one reflecting Stats. 2024, Ch. 361, Sec. 10, each itself building on a 2019 amendment); the quoted text above is drawn from, and independently double-fetched and confirmed against, the Sec. 9 version specifically, and the Sec. 10 version was not independently checked to confirm whether it states the quoted definition identically — a reader should not assume the two versions are necessarily identical in every respect. This clause states what these two statutes provide about the registered limited liability partnership form; it does not evaluate whether any specific person's or group's practice qualifies for that form, and does not address every other business-entity alternative (such as the professional corporation form, addressed in this project's separate Professional Corporation — Formation Information Sheet) that may be available to a given licensed profession. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and these requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
I, Jordan T. Reyes, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.04 and the statutes it cross-references, for informational reference only. This information sheet does not constitute legal advice, does not evaluate whether any specific profession or proposed business may lawfully use the limited liability company, professional corporation, or registered limited liability partnership form, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

Profession or field discussed, if applicable: Law

Business name under consideration, if applicable: Acme Consulting

Executed on September 3, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: ☐ _________________________

As of this verification, the California Legislative Information website listed two different 2024-amended versions of Section 16101 on file (one reflecting Stats. 2024, Ch. 361, Sec. 9, and a separate one reflecting Stats. 2024, Ch. 361, Sec. 10, each itself building on a 2019 amendment); the quoted text above is drawn from, and independently double-fetched and confirmed against, the Sec. 9 version specifically, and the Sec. 10 version was not independently checked to confirm whether it states the quoted definition identically — a reader should not assume the two versions are necessarily identical in every respect. This clause states what these two statutes provide about the registered limited liability partnership form; it does not evaluate whether any specific person's or group's practice qualifies for that form, and does not address every other business-entity alternative (such as the professional corporation form, addressed in this project's separate Professional Corporation — Formation Information Sheet) that may be available to a given licensed profession. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and these requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.
